plan.title: The rain gauge that failed
plan.concept: A student-built rain gauge overflows and fails its first monsoon-week test. Instead of a teacher fixing it, the students redesign it themselves over three days.
plan.copy: Their rain gauge failed on day one. They didn't throw it out.
plan.caption:
Their rain gauge failed on day one. They didn't throw it out.
 The container overflowed before noon on its very first test. The numbers it produced meant absolutely nothing.
 Instead of asking a teacher for the fix, four students sat down with the wreckage of their own design and asked one real question: what should this have looked like instead?
 Wider base. Marked intervals. A sloped lid to stop the splash-back. By Thursday afternoon, the redesigned gauge was sitting back out in the garden — built entirely by the same four hands that broke the first one.
 That's the entire point of the Curiosity Lab. A wrong answer isn't a delay in our timetable. It's the actual lesson plan.

plan.title: Learning beyond the blackboard
plan.concept: This video visually breaks down the myth that math is just about memorizing numbers and formulas on a blackboard. By jumping through different grade levels, it shows how the school actively changes its teaching style to match a child's age—moving from tactile blocks in nursery to hands-on logic in the math lab, and finally to deep conceptual theory in high school.
plan.copy:
What is the first thing you do to help students understand a math concept?
The Real, One-Line Everyday Answers:
Nursery & PP1:
We don't teach written numbers yet—we just practice simple counting using physical things they can touch, like pulses, grains, and blocks.
Primary School (Classes 1–2):
We use examples they live out every day—like calculating how many chocolates they have left after sharing some with a friend.
Middle School (Classes 5–6):
We take them directly into our Maths Lab so they can use physical materials to touch, feel, and understand the logic behind a formula.
High School (Classes 11–12):
Instead of telling them to just memorize a formula, we spend the first part of the lesson breaking down the actual theory and concept behind it.

plan.title: Keep turning the compass
plan.concept: This concept captures the raw, practical reality of a student mastering a compass through sheer repetition. We visually show the progression of a child trying, failing, adjusting their grip, and trying again on a single page until they finally get that perfect, continuous round line.
plan.copy:
Headline:
It takes a few tries to get it right.
Subline:
Behind every clean, continuous round line is a page full of erased marks and broken curves.
We let our students explore until the ends meet.
plan.caption:
The needle slips on the first try. The pencil lifts halfway through the second try. The first few attempts do not look like circles at all.
Using a compass for the first time is all about practice. A child has to learn how to keep the center needle completely still. At the same time, they have to rotate the pencil smoothly.
But they do not give up. They erase the broken lines, adjust their grip, and try again. The curiosity keeps them trying until the two ends of the line finally meet perfectly.
